solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Tie required in Oxford but not Wellington? (8)

annotation.definition: Tie required in Oxford but not Wellington?

blocks.note: reads as a college dress code; an Oxford is also a laced leather shoe
reads as a school or a duke; a Wellington is a rubber boot pulled on with no fastening

annotation.surface: A dress code that demands a tie at Oxford University but not at Wellington College.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford and Wellington read as a university and a school, but they are footwear, so the tie is the one that fastens a shoe.
annotation.definitionFit: The only tie an Oxford shoe needs and a Wellington boot lacks is the lace that fastens it.

entries.clue: Singer and old lady right at home (6)

annotation.surface: A singer who lives with their mother.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is slang for mother, not an elderly woman.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Dean Martin and Chris Martin are both famous singers.

entries.clue: Ripe romp could be seen as this (8)

annotation.definition: Ripe romp could be seen as this

indicatorNotes.could be seen as: the letters of the fodder can be looked at in another arrangement

annotation.surface: A bawdy frolic might strike some people as indecent.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the letters rearrange, and a ripe romp is exactly what might be judged indecent.
annotation.definitionFit: Ripe here means risqué, and a risqué romp is the very thing prudes call indecent, so the clue reads straight.

entries.clue: Charted road going north, east and west (4)

indicatorNotes.going north: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

annotation.surface: A map shows a road running in three compass directions.
annotation.walkthrough: The compass words look like the map's content, and each is just its letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To chart a coastline is to draw it on a map, so charted and drew share the mapping sense.

entries.clue: Transfix reader originally entertained by article? (6)

indicatorNotes.originally: the origin of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.entertained by: a host entertains a guest inside the home

blocks.note: a piece = an article, as in a newspaper piece
first letter of Reader, placed inside PIE|CE

annotation.surface: A reader is spellbound by something in the paper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Transfix' pretends to mean enthral, but here it means to run through; 'article' is a written piece, not a grammar word.
annotation.definitionFit: Transfix's literal sense is to run a spike right through something, which is to spear or impale it.

entries.clue: English boy raised in valley (4)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, lifting the letters up reads them backwards

annotation.surface: An English lad who grew up in the countryside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Raised' reads as brought up, as in childhood; here it flips ELAD upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional word: dale is the northern English name for a valley, as in the Yorkshire Dales.

entries.clue: One can’t fly after Heathrow checks (4)

indicatorNotes.checks: to check is to hold back, so the phrase holds the answer

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the first three of the second

annotation.surface: Someone is grounded after airport security at Heathrow.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is air travel, but the one who cannot fly is a bird; Heathrow is London's main airport.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the rhea is a large South American bird that cannot fly.

entries.clue: Constituency with small majority / in the Borders? (8)

blocks.note: British political jargon for a seat that could change hands at the next election
the borders of a page are its margins; the question mark flags the pun

annotation.surface: A closely fought parliamentary seat in the Scottish Borders.
annotation.walkthrough: The Borders is a Scottish region, which makes this sound like election geography; with a small b, borders are the margins of a page.
annotation.definitionFit: British politics calls a narrowly held seat a marginal, and anything in the margins of a page is marginal too.

entries.clue: Bully about to run after man (6)

indicatorNotes.after: the man comes first and the rest follows him

annotation.surface: A bully is about to chase after a man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as a single idea meaning going to, but it splits into C and TO.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are verbs; the word comes from Hector of Troy, whose name came to mean a swaggering browbeater.

entries.clue: Fighting almost tore apart densely populated area (6)

indicatorNotes.almost: not quite all the word: drop its last letter

blocks.note: REND (tore apart) without its last letter

annotation.surface: Conflict nearly destroyed a crowded district.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tore apart' looks like past-tense destruction; REND is the word it stands for.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative use from the rabbit's burrow system: a crowded maze of streets or rooms.

entries.clue: Beginnings of days always witnessed now? (4)

annotation.definition: Beginnings of days always witnessed now?

indicatorNotes.Beginnings of: the beginning of a word is its first letter, taken from each word that follows

blocks.note: one first letter from each of the four words

annotation.surface: Wondering whether the start of each day is always seen at the present moment.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: every day begins with first light, witnessed now.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes daybreak: the beginning of every day, seen as it arrives.

entries.clue: Play-acting up to age nine starts to create empathy (8)

indicatorNotes.starts to: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: pre-ten: a child of nine or under

annotation.surface: Young children use make-believe to learn empathy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up to age nine' is a playful way of saying pre-ten, a child not yet ten.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean putting on a false show, as an actor does.

entries.clue: Remove broadcast about all time to come (8)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: seeds broadcast are scattered in all directions

blocks.note: re = about, as in memo headers; joins the fodder

annotation.surface: An instruction to take something off the air for good.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like radio or TV, but it scatters REMOVE plus RE.
annotation.definitionFit: A poetic word, as in 'for evermore': ever onwards, through all the time still to come.

entries.clue: Type of punishment for petty officer (8)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Type of punishment' describes the adjective in corporal punishment

blocks.note: the kind inflicted on the body, from Latin corpus
petty = minor; wanted here is a junior army NCO rank

annotation.surface: Asking what penalty a junior naval officer should receive.
annotation.walkthrough: Petty officer is a naval rank, but here it just means a minor officer.
annotation.definitionFit: Corporal describes punishment of the body, and as a noun is a low army rank.

entries.clue: Wrong-headed way to read poetry? (8)

blocks.note: per = by way of, one verse at a time

annotation.surface: A contrary suggestion for how poems should be read.
annotation.walkthrough: Reading poetry per verse, one verse at a time, is sensible; the joke is that the phrase spells the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone wrong-headed insists on the contrary view, which is being perverse.

entries.clue: Truth is really breached by information technology (6)

indicatorNotes.breached by: a wall breached by something has it breaking in

blocks.note: IT = information technology, placed inside VER|Y

annotation.surface: The truth is badly compromised by computer systems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Really' reads as an intensifier but supplies VERY.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal synonym from Latin veritas, truth.

entries.clue: Spot check (4)

blocks.note: a spot or blemish on a surface
what a teacher does to homework

annotation.walkthrough: 'Spot check' reads as one phrase, a random inspection; split it into two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A mark is a spot on a surface, and marking work is checking it.

entries.clue: Tune millions yodel badly (6)

indicatorNotes.badly: done badly, the letters come out in the wrong order

annotation.surface: Millions of people yodel a tune out of key.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly' reads as a comment on the singing and is the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the air of a song, the part you hum.

entries.clue: 60 per cent of algorithms altered text praising God (6)

indicatorNotes.60 per cent of: ALGORITHMS has ten letters, so keep the first six
indicatorNotes.altered: the kept letters are changed around

blocks.note: first six of the ten letters of ALGORITHMS

annotation.surface: Computer code has tampered with a hymn.
annotation.walkthrough: The fraction is exact: six of ten letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The Gloria in excelsis Deo, 'glory to God in the highest', is the hymn of praise sung in the Mass.

entries.clue: Flower I planted in lines close to rockery (4)

indicatorNotes.planted in: put inside, as a bulb in soil
indicatorNotes.close to: the close of a word is its end, so take its last letter

annotation.surface: A gardener sets a flower in rows near the rock garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Planted' fits the gardening picture and is the container instruction; LL stands for lines, as in 'pp' for pages.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the lily is a garden flower grown from a bulb.

entries.clue: Land mass is receding within America’s borders (4)

indicatorNotes.receding: something receding moves back, so the word runs backwards
indicatorNotes.within: one word sits within another, inside its letters
indicatorNotes.borders: the outer letters of the word

blocks.note: first and last letters of AmericA

annotation.surface: Land is being lost inside the United States.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Receding' suggests coastal erosion, but it turns IS round.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a continent is a land mass, and Asia is the largest.

entries.clue: Military Intelligence officer in contact with poet (6)

blocks.note: MI = Military Intelligence, as in MI5

annotation.surface: An intelligence officer is in touch with a poet.
annotation.walkthrough: The spy story is all abbreviations; 'in contact with' means ON, as a hand on a table.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: John Milton wrote Paradise Lost.

entries.clue: I chortle about tailor (8)

annotation.surface: Someone laughs about a tailor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as concerning, but it asks for the letters to be moved about.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: both make or sell garments, the clothier more broadly.

entries.clue: Head of faculty’s area included in study (4)

indicatorNotes.included in: one thing included in another sits among its parts, here among its letters

blocks.note: a den = a study, a private room

annotation.surface: A faculty head's floor space is part of a research study.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Study' reads as research, but it is a room: a den.
annotation.definitionFit: The university title for the academic in charge of a faculty.
